title: Work with excellence
hook: a hadith: God loves that when you do a work, you do it with excellence (al-Bayhaqi)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was al-Bukhari, whose collection keeps the saying about food you earn with your own hands. Your line was bread you paid for. Today, the same tradition asks how the work is done.

The underside of a drawer. Nobody will ever see it. The customer opens the drawer, takes out a spoon, and never once turns it over. Still, some carpenters sand that hidden side as smooth as the front. A Muslim narration speaks to exactly this. It's recorded in the hadith collection of al-Bayhaqi, and it says, in paraphrase, that when one of you does a piece of work, God loves that it be done with excellence. Not the work people watch. Any work. Today's word names that kind of care.
screen: `THE UNDERSIDE OF A DRAWER.` → `NOBODY SEES IT.` → `GOD LOVES WORK DONE WELL.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Ihsan is Arabic, put into English as excellence, or doing what is beautiful. It comes up in a scene recorded in Sahih Muslim. A stranger in very white clothes sits knee to knee with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asks: what is islam? What is iman, faith? And what is ihsan? The answer, in paraphrase: to worship God as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, to know that He sees you. After the stranger leaves, the Prophet tells his companions it was the angel Gabriel, come to teach them their religion. So ihsan begins as a way of standing before God. Second, it doesn't stay in the prayer hall. Another hadith in Sahih Muslim says God has prescribed ihsan in all things, and its example is a knife: when you slaughter an animal, sharpen your blade and spare the animal. Third, the narration from al-Bayhaqi takes it into the workshop: God loves that when you do a work, you do it well. Muslim teachers describe ihsan as doing a thing as though it's seen, because, in their faith, it is. In that telling, the underside of the drawer is not hidden from God. Fourth, what this asks of an ordinary afternoon. Not perfectionism, the anxious kind that never finishes. Attention. The email read once more before sending. The bandage put on gently. Excellence, in this telling, is less about being the best and more about not cutting the corner nobody would notice.
screen: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.` · `IHSAN IN ALL THINGS.` · `GOD LOVES WORK DONE WELL.` · `ATTENTION, NOT PERFECTIONISM.` · then, large: `IHSAN.`

segments.voice: Make this sitting the piece of work: set your feet with care, let the back lengthen, and give each breath your full attention. When the mind wanders, come back without fuss, the way you'd sand one more stroke on a side nobody sees. If you pray, you can sit as though seen, in your own tradition's way; if you don't, simply let the breath have your care.
Ihsan. An Arabic word for excellence, doing what is beautiful, as though seen by God. Today's word.
Your line: excellence. Even on the side nobody turns over. Day eight hundred ninety-seven, done.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of ihsan both in worship, praying as though seeing God, and in daily work, and teachers often cite the hadith that God loves work done with excellence when talking about jobs, crafts and study.

notes: The al-Bayhaqi narration's Arabic verb is generally given as yutqinahu (from itqan, precision/excellence), not ihsan. The index word is ihsan, so the script ties the narration to ihsan through Sahih Muslim 8 and 1955 rather than claiming the narration uses the word ihsan. A Muslim Keeper should confirm this framing and the narration's grading.
Confirm hadith numbering: Sahih Muslim 8 (Gabriel: islam, iman, ihsan) and Sahih Muslim 1955 (God has prescribed ihsan in all things; sharpen the blade).
'A stranger in very white clothes ... knee to knee' paraphrases details of Sahih Muslim 8; confirm.
'Muslim teachers describe ihsan as doing a thing as though it's seen' is an attribution, not a count; confirm phrasing.
All hadith paraphrased; no English hadith translation quoted.
